title: The Business of War in the Central Sahel
summary: Maya and Daniel break down a landmark report from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime exploring how illicit economies fuel armed conflict across Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso. They examine the resurgence of foreign kidnap-for-ransom, the contestation of vital transport corridors, shifting artisanal gold and drug supply chains, and actionable entry points for policy intervention.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Welcome back. Today we are digging into a major report just released by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, titled The Business of War: Illicit Markets and Their Intersection with Conflict in the Central Sahel. If you follow West African security, counter-terrorism, or illicit finance, this report is essential reading because it maps how criminal economies and armed conflict have become completely intertwined across Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And what stands out right away is that the military regimes in Bamako, Niamey, and Ouagadougou promised restored sovereignty and security when they took power. But as GI-TOC documents, what is actually happening on the ground is fragmented state control, rising violence, and an illicit war economy that is becoming deeply entrenched. Conflict actors aren't just fighting; they are running businesses.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. The report makes the case that you cannot separate the military conflict from the illicit flows that resource it. Whether we are talking about artisanal gold, fuel, synthetic drugs, weapons, or hostages, these illicit economies provide armed groups with cash, operational supplies, and even local legitimacy.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let's start with one of the most eye-opening shifts in the report: the kidnap-for-ransom economy. For years, kidnapping foreigners in the Sahel seemed to have died down, especially during that lull in 2023 and 2024. But in 2025, it roared back.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. But the report draws a crucial distinction between two parallel kidnapping industries. On one hand, you have the localized kidnapping of Sahelian citizens. Between 2017 and August 2026, ninety-seven percent of all recorded kidnapping incidents in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger targeted local citizens—that is 1,776 events out of 1,835. Groups like JNIM use that largely for coercion, gathering intelligence, and enforcing local obedience, with ransoms demanded in only a fraction of cases.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Whereas the kidnapping of foreign nationals is purely about massive capital injection and geopolitical economic warfare. What is striking is how Islamic State Sahel Province, or IS Sahel, completely reversed its traditional playbook. Historically, they barely touched foreign kidnapping—only one recorded case back in 2018.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Until late 2024, when IS Sahel made a deliberate strategic pivot. They recruited seasoned bandits, created a dedicated hostage-taking unit, and used their consolidated territorial control over Mali's Ménaka region as a secure sanctuary where they can hold hostages long-term. Over the past year, they have seized at least ten foreign victims: Austrian, Spanish, Moroccan, Chinese, Swiss, and American nationals.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And look at the incentive structure they created for criminal networks. GI-TOC notes that IS Sahel offers local bandits between 130,000 and 350,000 euros for delivering a foreign captive. That has sparked cross-border kidnapping bounties. Remember that Spanish citizen taken in southern Algeria near Tamanrasset in January 2025? The kidnappers hauled him across the border through Tinzaouaten towards Ménaka, and he was only freed because the rebel FLA, the Azawad Liberation Front, intercepted the convoy before the handoff.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And the financial payoff for IS Sahel has been staggering. By mid-2026, the group is believed to have collected tens of millions of dollars for releasing American, Swiss, and Austrian hostages. That cash influx is already making them noticeably bolder in their military operations, particularly in clashes against JNIM.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Meanwhile, JNIM has restructured its own foreign kidnapping strategy. In southern Mali, they abducted some 22 foreign nationals in 2025, largely targeting Chinese and Indian workers from industrial mines and cement factories. It serves as economic warfare to frighten off foreign investment and bleed the military junta of mining taxes. But then in October 2025, JNIM pulled off the kidnapping of an Emirati royal family member, netting a reported fifty million dollar ransom.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Fifty million dollars. That single payout ranks among the largest ransoms ever paid for an individual. And UN reporting cited by GI-TOC indicates that proceeds from that kidnapping helped finance JNIM's massive coordinated attacks across Mali in April and July 2026, with funds also funneled back to al-Qaeda's core leadership and its affiliate in Yemen. At the same time, JNIM is being selective: they've largely stepped back from kidnapping Westerners to cultivate political legitimacy, focusing their abductions instead on citizens of states seen as aligned with the junta, like Egypt, Iran, the UAE, India, and China.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That brings us directly to the physical conduits of this war economy: the roads. The report emphasizes how armed groups have turned major transit corridors into choke points and theatres of economic warfare.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It really reframes how we look at transport infrastructure. In a mapping of 350 illicit hubs across West Africa and the Sahel, GI-TOC found that eighty-seven percent are located on or near major operational roads. Furthermore, the vast majority of violent conflict fatalities happen within a single kilometer of a road. In southern Mali, over ninety percent of JNIM attacks in 2025 occurred within ten kilometers of a major national highway.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: JNIM's sieges are not just random violence. As the report explains, they are a calculated governance tactic. By cutting off access routes, enforcing fuel blockades, and ambushing convoys on the Bamako-Dakar, Bamako-Abidjan, and Bamako-Conakry highways, JNIM isolates urban populations, forces communities into submission, and chokes the junta's economic lifeline without taking on the burden of providing public services.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: We see the exact same logic in Niger. In Tillabéri, which has become the deadliest region in the central Sahel—accounting for nearly 1,300 of the roughly 1,940 conflict deaths recorded in Niger in 2025—about seventy percent of IS Sahel's attacks on civilians occurred within 24 kilometers of the N1 or N23 highways connecting to Niamey. And their major attacks on military bases, like the June 2026 raids on Inatès and Banibangou that killed 85 Nigerien soldiers, were right along these primary corridors.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Yet along these same corridors, armed groups also build predatory protection economies. In Ménaka, instead of just looting cattle like they used to, IS Sahel now runs a structured taxation system, charging pastoralist villages an annual grazing tax between 500,000 and three million CFA francs in exchange for protection against bandits and JNIM.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Which brings us to what might be the economic backbone of the entire conflict ecosystem: artisanal and small-scale gold mining, or ASGM. The sheer scale here is breathtaking. In Mali alone, the Council of Ministers reported nearly two million people employed across 350 to 400 artisanal gold sites as of June 2026. In Niger, over 800,000 people depend on it.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the volumes of undeclared gold moving through illicit channels dwarf the official figures. Mali officially declares about six tonnes of artisanal gold annually, but SWISSAID estimates that another thirty to fifty-seven tonnes leave the country undeclared every year, meaning total production is between 36 and 63 tonnes.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: What is alarming now is JNIM's southward push into Mali's primary gold belts in Kayes and Sikasso. Kayes alone accounts for eighty percent of Mali's national gold production. Historically, JNIM operated around remote northern artisanal sites. In the south, they don't seize the mines directly; they negotiate monthly cash cuts with local site managers, the tomboloma. These youth associations collect about ten percent from miners and hand half of that—so roughly five percent of total site earnings—directly to JNIM.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And by positioning themselves in Kayes and Sikasso, JNIM isn't just skimming artisanal pits; they are actively threatening the logistics and contractors of industrial, foreign-owned mines, attacking sites like Morila, Bereko, and Kolenda, destroying equipment to escalate economic pressure.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: At the same time, this entire gold economy is deeply plugged into global markets, which makes it vulnerable to external shocks. A fascinating detail in the report is what happened in March 2026 when conflict broke out in Iran. The airspace over Dubai—which is where nearly all illicit West African gold laundered through Bamako's 140 gold trading comptoirs ends up—was severely disrupted. In the immediate aftermath, mine-site gold prices across the Sahel collapsed from their normal 75 to 90 percent of the global spot price down to just sixty percent.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Miners took the brunt of that crash, with some buyers halting purchases altogether. That volatility highlights the fragile link between Sahelian conflict financing and Gulf markets. Meanwhile, the military governments are desperately trying to assert state control over mineral rents, but they are doing so through deeply compromised partnerships. Look at the refinery deals.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, two of the state refinery projects involve heavily sanctioned entities. In Mali, the state partnered with Russia's Yadran Group, an EU-sanctioned entity, on a refinery in Bamako slated for completion in early 2027. And in Niger, the regime launched Royal Gold Niger SA in April 2025 with a Dubai entity whose CEO is Kamlesh Pattni Mansukhlal Damji, an individual sanctioned by both the US and the UK for running transnational gold smuggling and money laundering networks.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: It's incredible: putting a sanctioned gold smuggler at the helm of your national gold formalization initiative. Any international bank or trader dealing with those flows faces immediate secondary sanctions exposure, which virtually guarantees that Niger's gold will continue flowing directly into the illicit shadow economy.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And it isn't just gold. Niger's petroleum and uranium sectors are under intense strain. In the east, ISWAP raids around the Lake Chad basin threaten the Agadem oil zone. And the anti-junta rebel group, the Patriotic Movement for Freedom and Justice, or MPLJ, has launched repeated attacks on the Agadem-Dibella oil facilities and the Niger-Benin export pipeline, explicitly trying to choke off the junta's oil revenue, forcing the China National Petroleum Corporation to suspend operations and evacuate workers.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let's turn to logistics and the arms trade, because the report outlines how weapons trafficking has fused with other commodities since the war in Sudan erupted in April 2023.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The Sudan war has acted as a massive engine for regional instability. In mid-2023, hundreds of Chadian fighters left southern Libya to join the Rapid Support Forces, or RSF. Weapons and military hardware flown into Nyala, Abéché, and N'Djamena have started spilling outward across the Sahel. Soviet-pattern heavy machine guns, automatic rifles, and RPGs are flowing across Chad and Libya right into the hands of JNIM and IS Sahel.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the report emphasizes that arms trafficking doesn't happen in a silo anymore. Weapons, fuel, stolen vehicles, and armed combatants travel in fused convoys managed by the same brokers. Even communications technology has become part of this illicit bundle. The widespread adoption of illicit Starlink satellite terminals allows traffickers and armed groups to coordinate movements, payments, and checkpoints in remote desert expanses where mobile networks don't exist.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: You also see foreign mercenaries embedding themselves and transferring advanced capabilities. The report mentions Russian Africa Corps personnel operating alongside RSF-linked forces in southern Libya, while Colombian ex-military contractors were funneled through Benghazi and Kufra into Darfur by private UAE-linked security channels.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What about human smuggling? The findings here surprised me. The authors note that violent extremist groups do not systematically control or profit from human smuggling along migration routes, contrary to what many assume.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. While low-level extortion occurs, VEOs aren't running human smuggling syndicates. However, armed conflict has dramatically restructured migration geography. For decades, the primary overland pipeline ran from coastal West Africa through Ouagadougou to Niamey, and north to Libya. But persistent VEO attacks on commercial buses along routes like Dori-Téra forced transport companies to divert entirely through Togo and Benin, crossing at Malanville and Gaya.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And when the Benin-Niger border closed following the 2023 Niger coup, moving along that corridor became far more expensive and dangerous. At the same time, intensified fighting in northern Mali cut off the route to Algeria, reducing migrant transit through Timbuktu by an estimated thirty percent. That combination of overland blockages pushed thousands of migrants toward the maritime Atlantic route, triggering record arrivals of over 40,000 and 46,000 people to the Canary Islands in 2023 and 2024.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And increasingly, those moving through these ecosystems are not just economic migrants, but refugees fleeing Sudan—leaving camps in eastern Chad to work on dangerous goldfields in northern Chad, Niger, and Mali, or heading north toward the Mediterranean.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: We also need to touch on drug markets, because trans-Sahelian cocaine trafficking is reviving, and synthetic drugs are exploding. On cocaine, the seizure of 278 kilograms in Zinder in eastern Niger showed that maritime coastal flows from places like Ghana are still moving northward across the desert toward Libya.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And local protection rackets are adapting. In Niger, the pro-junta civilian militia known as the UNVP, the Union of Nigeriens for Vigilance and Patriotism, has emerged as an active facilitator, providing escort and recovery services for drug convoys. In Mali, following the army's northward push, cocaine trafficking shifted into Ménaka, where the powerful Tilemsi trafficking network struck a deal with IS Sahel to escort cocaine shipments from Talataye into Niger.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And on synthetics, the landscape is deteriorating rapidly. It used to be just diverted tramadol. Now the region is flooded with counterfeit pharmaceuticals like pregabalin, marketed as Lyrica, and the dangerous synthetic drug kush, which is expanding in southern Mali and Senegal. In coastal states, kush has been found to contain deadly nitazene opioids and synthetic cannabinoids, and there is grave concern that the same lethal mix is taking hold in the Sahel.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Plus the emergence of captagon. Nigeria's NDLEA confirmed captagon tablets in an April 2026 seizure, and networks in northern Nigeria, particularly Kano, are reportedly buying pills stamped with 'Lamborghini' logos to smuggle overland via the Sahel into Libya, Egypt, and the Middle East.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Given this grim diagnostic, what does the report actually recommend? What are the entry points for policymakers and international partners?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The report focuses on four specific, realistic interventions. First, capitalize on the market shock from the Iran conflict to intervene in the artisanal gold sector. Because the UAE market was disrupted and informal gold prices plummeted, regional states and formal buyers have a brief window to offer competitive pricing, formal finance, and long-term buyer relationships to ASGM miners, pulling gold away from illicit networks and VEO taxation.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Second, they call for dynamic monitoring of illicit economies to rebuild situational awareness. Following the withdrawal of the UN mission MINUSMA and shrinking civic space, information on rural illicit markets has degraded. Without granular data on price shifts and trafficking routes, early warning is impossible.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Third, international actors should use targeted sanctions strategically—not just on high-profile warlords who don't care, but on the private-sector facilitators, logistics brokers, and commercial fixers who negotiate company protection deals or facilitate cocaine and hostage ransoms. And fourth, rapidly step up regional coordination and forensic intelligence-sharing on synthetic drugs, building on initiatives like the November 2025 Accra Call to Action to stop nitazenes and captagon from gaining a permanent foothold.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Looking ahead, what are the key milestones to watch in the coming months?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Keep a close eye on the Benin-Niger border talks. Beninese President Romuald Wadagni visited Niamey in June 2026 to negotiate reopening the border with President Tiani. If that border reopens, it will immediately shift the eastern smuggling corridors and migration routes. Also watch the gold refinery projects in Bamako and Niamey, the potential spillover of surplus arms if fighting in Sudan shifts, and whether JNIM tries to replicate its Mali-style road and fuel blockades around Niamey. The bottom line from GI-TOC is clear: you cannot stabilize the Central Sahel with military force alone while leaving the war economies that sustain it completely untouched.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: A sobering but vital analysis. You can read the full report, The Business of War, on the Global Initiative website. Thank you for listening, and we'll see you next time.
